knitr::opts_chunk$set(

library(mvgam)

Species are often monitored by several protocols at once. A structured
count route, an occupancy survey and opportunistic sightings each
observe the same underlying intensity of individuals, filtered through
a different sampling process. Integrated distribution models fit one
likelihood per protocol and tie every likelihood to that shared
intensity (Fithian et al.
[2015](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12242); Isaac et al.
[2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tree.2019.08.006); Miller et al.
[2019](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13110)). Each protocol then
informs the environmental response that drives the intensity.

mvgam fits such a model as a multivariate formula. Each protocol gets
its own `bf()` with the family and link that describe its sampling
process. One `trend_formula` describes the log-intensity they share.
This article simulates three protocols observing one species, then
compares how well the joint model and each protocol alone recover the
species' response to an environmental gradient. The article on
[one latent process with several observation models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/mvbf.html)
covers the same machinery from the angle of the latent state.

## The data

We simulate one species observed monthly for eight years. Its
log-intensity combines a bell-shaped response $f$ to an environmental
index with an autoregression at lags 1 and 12:

$$
\log \lambda_t = \alpha + f(\text{env}_t) + z_t, \qquad
z_t \sim \mathrm{Normal}(\phi_1 z_{t-1} + \phi_{12} z_{t-12},\ \sigma),
$$

with $\phi_1 = 0.55$, $\phi_{12} = 0.30$ and $\sigma = 0.35$. The
response $f$ peaks at env $= 0.4$.

Each protocol links to $\lambda_t$ through its own sampling process.
Counts along a route surveyed with effort $E_t$ are Poisson with mean
$\lambda_t E_t$. The term `offset(log_effort)` carries the effort. An
occupancy survey of a plot of area $A$ detects the species when at
least one individual is present. With a Poisson number of individuals
in the plot, the detection probability is $p_t = 1 - \exp(-\lambda_t
A)$. This is the inverse complementary log-log link, under which
$\text{cloglog}(p_t) = \log \lambda_t + \log A$ (McCullagh and Nelder
[1989](https://doi.org/10.1201/9780203753736)). With
`bernoulli(link = "cloglog")`, the occupancy record shares the
log-intensity of the counts, offset by $\log A$. Opportunistic
sightings arrive at rate $\lambda_t$ thinned by an unknown, constant
observer effort. Treated as a thinned Poisson process, they take a
free intercept that absorbs the log thinning and leaves the shape of
$f$ identified (Fithian et al.
[2015](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12242); Renner et al.
[2015](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12352)).

```{r simulate}
set.seed(2026)
n_t <- 96
env <- as.numeric(scale(cumsum(rnorm(n_t, 0, 0.3))))
f_env <- function(x) 1.5 * exp(-0.5 * (x - 0.4)^2) - 0.4

z <- numeric(n_t)
for (t in seq_len(n_t)) {
  z[t] <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.35) +
    (if (t > 1) 0.55 * z[t - 1] else 0) +
    (if (t > 12) 0.30 * z[t - 12] else 0)
}
lambda <- exp(0.5 + f_env(env) + z)

effort <- runif(n_t, 0.5, 2)
area <- 0.25
log_thinning <- -0.8

idm_data <- data.frame(
  time = seq_len(n_t),
  series = factor("species1"),
  env = env,
  log_effort = log(effort),
  count = rpois(n_t, lambda * effort),
  pa = rbinom(n_t, 1, 1 - exp(-lambda * area)),
  po = rpois(n_t, lambda * exp(log_thinning))
)
```

## The joint model

The three `bf()` calls share the trend formula, which holds a smooth
of env and the autoregression at lags 1 and 12:

```{r joint-fit}
joint_formula <-
  bf(count ~ 1 + offset(log_effort), family = poisson()) +
  bf(pa ~ 1, family = bernoulli(link = "cloglog")) +
  bf(po ~ 1, family = poisson())
trend_formula <- ~ s(env, k = 8) + AR(p = c(1, 12))

mod_joint <- mvgam(
  joint_formula,
  trend_formula = trend_formula,
  data = idm_data,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  chains = 4, seed = 2026, silent = 2
)
```

`plot(type = "series")` draws each protocol's record, its
distribution and its autocorrelation:

```{r series, fig.asp = 1.25, fig.cap = "The three simulated records: counts, occupancy detections and opportunistic sightings."}
plot(mod_joint, type = "series")
```

`summary()` reports one intercept per protocol and the trend
parameters they share:

```{r summary}
summary(mod_joint)
```

```{r trend-numbers, include = FALSE}
ar12 <- as.numeric(as_draws_matrix(mod_joint, variable = "ar12_trend[1]"))
fe_ar12 <- sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", median(ar12),
                   quantile(ar12, 0.025), quantile(ar12, 0.975))
```

The autoregressive coefficients and the innovation SD each cover the
values used to simulate the data. Because only eight annual cycles
inform it, the lag-12 coefficient (`r fe_ar12`) is the least certain of
these.

The intercepts carry what the shared trend leaves to each protocol.
Because the linear predictor of every protocol holds the same
$\log \lambda_t$, the trend cancels from the difference between two
intercepts. The difference between the occupancy and count intercepts
estimates $\log A$. The difference between the sightings and count
intercepts estimates the log thinning:

```{r contrasts}
b <- as_draws_df(
  mod_joint,
  variable = c("b_count_Intercept", "b_pa_Intercept", "b_po_Intercept")
)
contrasts <- data.frame(
  `log area` = b$b_pa_Intercept - b$b_count_Intercept,
  `log thinning` = b$b_po_Intercept - b$b_count_Intercept,
  check.names = FALSE
)
round(t(apply(contrasts, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))), 2)
```

```{r contrast-numbers, include = FALSE}
ci <- apply(contrasts, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
# The prose below says both intervals cover the simulated constants
stopifnot(ci[1, 1] < log(area), ci[2, 1] > log(area),
          ci[1, 2] < log_thinning, ci[2, 2] > log_thinning)
```

Both intervals cover the simulated constants, $\log 0.25 = -1.39$ and
$-0.8$. Neither constant was given to the model.

`pp_check()` draws one panel per protocol, with bars for the binary
occupancy record:

```{r ppc, fig.asp = 1, fig.cap = "Posterior predictive checks for each protocol."}
pp_check(mod_joint, ndraws = 50)
```

## The environmental response

`plot(type = "smooths")` draws the smooth of env on the log-intensity
scale:

```{r smooth, fig.cap = "The smooth of env from the joint model, with its 95% credible interval."}
plot(mod_joint, type = "smooths")
```

`conditional_effects()` carries that smooth through each protocol's
observation model, with the trend state held out and effort set to one:

```{r effects, fig.width = 9, fig.asp = 0.4, out.width = "95%", fig.cap = "Expected count, detection probability and sighting rate along env from the joint model, with 95% credible intervals."}
ce <- conditional_effects(mod_joint)
patchwork::wrap_plots(plot(ce, plot = FALSE), nrow = 1)
```

To ask what the integration gains, we fit each protocol alone with the
same trend formula:

```{r separate-fits}
fit_one <- function(formula) {
  mvgam(formula, trend_formula = trend_formula, data = idm_data,
        control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
        chains = 4, seed = 2026, silent = 2)
}
mod_count <- fit_one(
  bf(count ~ 1 + offset(log_effort), family = poisson())
)
mod_pa <- fit_one(bf(pa ~ 1, family = bernoulli(link = "cloglog")))
mod_po <- fit_one(bf(po ~ 1, family = poisson()))
```

Each model's linear predictor over a grid of env values shares the
shape of $f$. Subtracting its value at the median of the grid removes
the protocol's intercept and the trend state. The joint model's
predictor is taken from the count response:

```{r response-curves}
grid <- seq(min(env), max(env), length.out = 60)
ref <- which.min(abs(grid - median(grid)))
newdata <- idm_data[rep(1, length(grid)), ]
newdata$env <- grid
newdata$log_effort <- 0

response_draws <- function(fit, resp = NULL) {
  lp <- posterior_linpred(fit, newdata = newdata, resp = resp)
  lp - lp[, ref]
}
fits <- list(
  "Joint" = response_draws(mod_joint, resp = "count"),
  "Counts alone" = response_draws(mod_count),
  "Occupancy alone" = response_draws(mod_pa),
  "Sightings alone" = response_draws(mod_po)
)
truth <- data.frame(env = grid, f = f_env(grid) - f_env(grid[ref]))
curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(nm) {
  q <- apply(fits[[nm]], 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
  data.frame(model = nm, env = grid, lo = q[1, ], med = q[2, ],
             hi = q[3, ])
}))
curves$model <- factor(curves$model, levels = names(fits))
```

```{r response-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.asp = 0.62, out.width = "95%", fig.cap = "Posterior medians and 95% credible intervals of the response to env from the joint model and from each protocol alone. The black line is the simulated response."}
ggplot(curves, aes(env)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#DCBCBC") +
  geom_line(aes(y = med), colour = "#8F2727", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = f), data = truth, linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  labs(x = "env", y = "Shift in log-intensity")
```

Three summaries compare the four curves: the root mean squared error
of the posterior median against the simulated response, the mean width
of the 95% credible interval and the posterior median of the env value
at which each curve peaks.

```{r recovery-table}
recovery <- t(vapply(fits, function(draws) {
  q <- apply(draws, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975))
  peak <- grid[apply(draws, 1, which.max)]
  c(RMSE = sqrt(mean((q[2, ] - truth$f)^2)),
    `Interval width` = mean(q[3, ] - q[1, ]),
    `Peak env` = median(peak))
}, numeric(3)))
round(recovery, 2)
```

```{r recovery-numbers, include = FALSE}
fe <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
# The prose below says the joint model has the narrowest intervals, is
# more accurate than occupancy or sightings alone, and that occupancy
# alone puts the peak at the top of the observed range, and sightings
# alone well above the simulated optimum
stopifnot(which.min(recovery[, "Interval width"]) == 1,
          all(recovery[1, "RMSE"] < recovery[3:4, "RMSE"]),
          recovery["Occupancy alone", "Peak env"] == max(grid),
          recovery["Sightings alone", "Peak env"] > 0.6)
```

The joint model and the counts alone track the response about equally
closely, with root mean squared errors of
`r fe(recovery["Joint", "RMSE"])` and
`r fe(recovery["Counts alone", "RMSE"])`. The joint model's intervals
are the narrowest of the four. The sightings alone put the peak at env
`r fe(recovery["Sightings alone", "Peak env"])`, well above the
simulated optimum of 0.4. Because one binary
outcome per month constrains the intensity weakly, the occupancy record
alone estimates a response that rises across the whole gradient, with
its peak at the upper edge of the observed range.

## Forecasts

`forecast()` extends the shared state past the last month and passes it
through each protocol's observation model. The new data hold unit
effort and env at its final observed value. `type = "expected"`
returns the expected count, the detection probability and the expected
sightings:

```{r forecast, fig.asp = 1, fig.cap = "Expected values for each protocol over the training months and a 12-month forecast. Points are the observations."}
future <- data.frame(
  time = n_t + 1:12,
  series = factor("species1"),
  env = env[n_t],
  log_effort = 0,
  count = NA, pa = NA, po = NA
)
fc <- forecast(mod_joint, newdata = future, type = "expected")
plot(fc)
```

The three forecasts share one future for the state. Once the held-out
records arrive, `score()` evaluates them protocol by protocol.

## When protocols disagree

We fit the joint model on the premise that every protocol observes
one intensity through one response to env. Two violations are common.
The first is a mismatch of species. An opportunistic record that mixes
the target with an easily confused congener observes a different
intensity (Fithian et al.
[2015](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12242) analyse this case).
The second is a mismatch of habitat. If the occupancy plots sample
habitat the count route never visits, the two protocols see different
responses to env. A joint smooth then averages them.

The single-protocol fits diagnose both mismatches. A protocol whose response disagrees with
the others, beyond what its interval allows, is a candidate for a
response of its own. That response moves to the protocol's observation
formula, for example
`bf(pa ~ 1 + s(env, k = 5), family = bernoulli(link = "cloglog"))`,
while the shared response stays in the trend formula. Koshkina et al.
([2017](https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12738)) develop this
combination of presence-background and occupancy data with imperfect
detection.

## Summary

An integrated distribution model in mvgam is one call. Each protocol's
family and link express its sampling process. The shared trend pools
what every protocol says about the intensity. In this simulation,
pooling gave the most precise estimate of the environmental response,
as accurate as the best protocol alone. Because occupancy alone put the optimum in the wrong
habitat, that record gained the most from pooling.

## Where to next

Each function used here has a help page, such as `?pp_check` or
`?AR`, with its arguments and output. `how_to_cite()` writes a methods
paragraph for a fitted model. `methods_md()` writes out its equations.

Related articles:

- [One latent process, several observation models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/mvbf.html)
  compares the latent state recovered by joint and separate fits.
- [N-mixture models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/nmix.html)
  estimate detection from repeated visits within one protocol.
- [Joint species distribution models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/jsdgam.html)
  share latent factors among many species.
- [Forecast evaluation](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/forecast_evaluation.html)
  covers scoring rules and leave-future-out cross-validation.
